progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: pathogens and hosts, fungi as a group, plants are hosts too. From b03: indirect transmission by soil, water and fomites; control matches the route. From b04: introduced pathogens meet hosts with little resistance (myrtle rust); a disease can damage ecosystems as well as farms. From bio-m5-b02b: the plant reproduction context only (it assumes, and does not teach, roots or root tips). From Year 11: cell walls of cellulose; roots take up water; xylem carries it up. Not assumed: the root tip zones, oomycetes, zoospores, lignin, suberin, callose, phytoalexins, the hypersensitive response, always-there against switched-on defences, how to read an inoculation study.
progression.startsWith: Use a named plant and pathogen. The video opens: On many bush tracks in south-western Australia, there are boot-cleaning stations.
progression.stopsAfter: describing how *P. cinnamomi* (a water mould, not a fungus) infects roots (swimming spores attracted to roots, hyphae through the root, root death, wilting from the roots up) and spreads (water, soil on boots and tyres); explaining why a plant defends cell by cell; distinguishing defences that are always there (lignin and suberin in older root walls, bark; the young root behind the tip as the weak point, entered where two cells meet) from those switched on after detection (callose plugs, extra lignin, antimicrobial chemicals such as phytoalexins); explaining the hypersensitive response as a firebreak against a pathogen that needs living cells; tracing the published observations for scarlet banksia and old man banksia to a difference in timing, and naming the limits of that evidence (seedlings, laboratory, one study, tolerance not immunity); explaining why hygiene and phosphite fit this pathogen; interpreting unseen inoculation data and evaluating a claim about a dead spot.
progression.nextLesson: what happens first when a pathogen gets into an animal (route entry bio-m7-b06).

teaching.task: Plants can't send immune cells to an infection. So how does a banksia defend its roots against Phytophthora, and why does one species hold out while another dies?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why the plant wilts (roots die, less water up; scene 2); why a plant defends cell by cell (no circulating immune cells; scene 3); why the root tip is the weak point (thin young walls, no bark, while older walls toughen with age; scene 4); where the hypha gets in (usually where two cells meet; scene 4); how callose stops a hypha (a plug where it pushes in; scene 5); why cell death helps (a pathogen that needs living cells has nothing to feed on; scene 6); why one banksia held out (both laid down callose; the clearest difference the study reports is timing; scenes 7 and 8); why a short shared history is not "no defence" (old man banksia held it back; scene 9); why phosphite helps (faster walls, not soil removal; scene 10). Visible case: spores homing on the root, the cell pair revealing each defence in place, the seedling triplet racing on the day line. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scene 7 is the densest (two rows, five ticks), so only the row being spoken about is bright.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Boot-cleaning stations stand on bush tracks in south-western Australia because Phytophthora cinnamomi lives in the soil and about 40 per cent of the region's native plant species are susceptible, yet some banksias cope far better than others, so the question is how a plant with no immune cells defends itself and why one banksia holds out while another dies. The attacker is a water mould, not a fungus, whose swimming spores settle behind the root tip and grow hyphae that kill root tissue so less water reaches the leaves. Because no defender cells travel to the site, every cell defends itself, with barriers that are always there (lignin and other waterproof materials in older walls and bark, leaving the young root least protected) and responses switched on after detection (callose plugs, extra lignin and phytoalexins), and the hypersensitive response as a firebreak of deliberately dead cells around a pathogen that feeds on living cells. The 1998 seedling study compares scarlet banksia and old man banksia, timing is the clearest difference, and the evidence limits are named (seedlings, a lab, one study, tolerant not immune, an introduced pathogen). Hygiene and phosphite match the control to the defence, and the memory aid is that the hypersensitive response is a firebreak. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: On many bush tracks in south-western Australia, there are boot-cleaning stations. The reason is in the soil: Phytophthora cinnamomi, a pathogen that about 40 per cent of the region's native plant species are susceptible to. Yet some banksia species cope with it far better than others. So how does a plant with no immune cells defend itself, and why does one banksia hold out while another dies?
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a interprets hypothetical inoculation data for two species (callose timing and dead-zone length) and explains the response (the route's stop: explain barrier and chemical responses with evidence). 12c evaluates a claim that a small, stable dead spot means the defence has failed (the hypersensitive response, the site's misconception). Revision 3 (Codex check 100): the stem names a fungus that can feed only on living cells and gives rapid cell death within hours as evidence, because a stable spot alone does not identify the defence, and cell death can help a pathogen that feeds on dead tissue. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reason, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ2-01: "investigate the response of a named Australian plant to a named pathogen through practical and/or secondary-sourced investigation, for example:", with its listed examples "fungal pathogens" and "viral pathogens". The listed examples are "for example"; P. cinnamomi is a fungus-like oomycete, so it is not one of the two listed examples, but it is a named pathogen of named Australian plants, and the site uses it. The investigation is secondary-sourced (scenes 7 to 9): published observations are traced to the plant's responses and their limits are named. Verb "investigate" (plan, inquire into and draw conclusions about): examined, per the site's Explain model, as explain a named response with evidence; both attempts use evidence.

design.visualSystem: One defence race board. Left two-thirds: painted root and cell plates on which each defence is shown in place. Right third: a coded defence ladder of three rungs, filled as taught: "barriers: always there" (scene 4), "switched on: after detection" (scene 5), "firebreak: cells die" (scene 6). In scenes 7 and 8 the board becomes a race strip: a coded day line (day 0, 1, 3, 5, 9, as small grey ticks; no invented values between ticks) with two rows, one per species, each row carrying an aligned seedling plate that crossfades to its observed state at the ticks the study reports. Diseased against healthy plates are aligned pairs or triplets that crossfade (the banksia pair; the root cell triplet; the seedling triplet). The banksia pair uses the side-by-side fallback until its retake arrives (next bullet). No people, hands, faces, walkers or rangers: tracks and hygiene are shown by the boot-cleaning station alone. Coded elements are abstract only: the ladder, the day line, chips, arrows, swimming-path dotted lines and a signal pulse along a stem in scene 6. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
